Not giving up my details like field of work etc but vaguely: I did science and now I work on crime.

First time posting an EDC. I've got my old EDC first and then a "starter set" of sorts I've put together for myself more recently.

The first image shows my EDC as a postgrad as I went through two MSc programs one after another (one to qualify for grants, one to chance field). The second is my EDC in my current position as a researcher/writer. I work from home mostly now so the needs have changed.

I commuted via bike during this time so carried simple tools for maintenance in my bag at this time. I'd also have things like inner tubes and pump.

-1. Victorinox Climber Swiss Army Knife 1370330 VICCLIMBLACK

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Victorinox-Climber-Swiss-1370330-VICCLIMBLACK/dp/B0001P14WC/ I originally to one in the classic red look but it was stolen. I replaced it with this which covers basically all my common needs. The only thing I regret not having on this is the saw tool. But balancing size with utility this is basically perfect as far as I'm concerned.

-2. Cruzer Fit 16 GB USB 2.0 Flash Drive

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Cruzer-Fit-Flash-Drive-SDCZ33-016G-B35/dp/B005FYNSZA/ This is just big enough to hold a few very important things. Key peices of work. A bootable Linux installation (pre-configured). A portable installation of Firefox and a Zotero (reference manager) directory that pFirefox is pointed at. The Zotero-Firefox combo meant I could take EVERY SINGLE one of my journals/books with me to any work computer AND all my notes on them. I'll be upgrading this to a 3.0 version with 32 or 64gb when 3.0 becomes more common place.

-3. Molskine Sketchbook

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Moleskine-S01151-Sketchbook/dp/8883701151/ I've worked almost completely digitally since around 2000. I don't often take any notes. However, if I need to jot down dates, numbers or important info; I find tablets and phones are still just a little too clumsy and laptops are inconvenient if you don't have them out already. So I always have a notebook and I use it for sparse but important notes. Though I use it almost daily, it's taken me about 3 years to fill this. I'll replace it with the exact same type but soft-cover this time.

-4. Draper Allen Key Set

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Advanced-Draper-XS14128-Imperial-Warranty/dp/B00UQ890F2/ Not sure on the exact model of this because the code has worn off and, though it looks the same, what numbers are left don't match this link. But it's basically the same. Used for the bike. Hard-wearing and good range of sizes.

-5. Rolson 12 in 1 Deluxe Pocket Multi-Tool with Belt Pouch

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Rolson-Deluxe-Pocket-Multi-Tool-Pouch/dp/B00935N5XM Cheap quality. A freebie I was gifted after a friend got it thrown in with another purchase. I use it primarily for the pliers to adjust things like break cables. It's not nice to use or particularly resilient but it does the job and you get what you pay for. It's the thing I use the least and can least justify purchasing a nicer model just for the sake of having something nicer to do the same job so it stays. I'm not sure what the legal status of carrying this is as it doesn't lock but I have seen people mention trouble with multi-tools that close back up over where the blade extends from.

-6. Zebra M-301 0.5mm Stainless Steel Mechanical Pencil

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Zebra-M-301-Stainless-Mechanical-Pencil/dp/B00E8D8H50/ I prefer pencil to pen and metal to wood. This was picked because it was what on offer when I needed one rather than because it's any good. It works. I'm looking at getting one of these instead as they seem highly recommended: http://www.amazon.co.uk/Uni-Roulette-Rotation-Mechanical-Pencil/dp/B004OHNTVC/

The second image contains my current EDC (sort of). Apologies for weird numbering but it keeps the original items numbered the same.

1, 2, 3, and 6 as before. As I'm mostly working from home now the tools are gone, though they're still around, and I'll take them out if I'm out on the bike.

-4. Samsung Galaxy S4 I9505 with Anker 7800mAh Extended Battery

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Samsung-Galaxy-I9505-Black-unlocked/dp/B00I51EZ7A/ http://www.amazon.co.uk/7800mAh-Extended-Battery-Samsung-Aactive/dp/B00LO8T6VQ/ This was my first proper smart phone after getting actual funding/work and it's revolutionised how I organise my time. I still use the notepad and pencil to jot down important stuff but once it's added to a computer/phone/online the phone makes a perfect too for getting it all back out. I had a ZeroLemon 7500 mAh battery before the Anker one but it finally started to lose charge a little faster after almost two years. These do significantly increase the size and weight of the phone (which I actually really like). But it's the difference between 1 day if lucky/half a day of heavy use to 3-4 days of heavy use with everything turned on/up to max. I would never buy a phone in future for which I couldn't use an extended battery.

-5. Wallet

Simple leather wallet, unbranded and received as a gift so no idea where it's from. I enhanced the card behind the window a little so it was readable. Pope Card; should you wish to possess your own: http://i.imgur.com/WUqikTI.gif I also carry a "survival" (lol) card in the wallet. Basically one of these: http://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B006FTF9BA/ Not hugely useful but if you've got access to nothing else it's better than nothing.

-7. Lansky LKN333

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Lansky-Sharpeners-LKN333-World-Legal/dp/B00IJ93WW2/ To be clear: THIS IS NOT AN EVERYDAY CARRY. Whilst the knife is technically UK legal I suspect that it looks way too aggressive to not be confiscated on sight or worse. If I'm out and about I probably have the Swiss as those are generally acceptable (though I've still received shocked gasps on producing the Swiss for someone to borrow some scissors). If I'm going to the woods for the day/weekend I would take this. Certainly it's by me when I work from home.

-8. PXS-14 Southord 14 Piece Lock Pick Set

http://www.amazon.co.uk/PXS-14-SouthOrd-Piece-Lock-Pick/dp/B00GQ765R8/
I'll detail this below as I think everyone should own one of these even if they don't EDC it.

Some caveats here: you can get in trouble for having one of these if you look a bit shifty and might get charged with "Going equipped..." or something to that effect. Some places around the world do restrict ownership. In the UK, so long as you're not operating for money without a locksmith liscence or otherwise causing trouble you should be good. If I have my backpack, there is a good chance these are in a side pocket. The simplest thing to do is to carry some spare locks with it as "locksport" is a thing and I frequently play/practice with these without trouble. Far more acceptable than carrying a knife in my experience.

-9. ThruNite T30S V2

http://www.amazon.co.uk/ThruNite®-T30S-V2-Momentay--Multifunctional/dp/B00N8MNIJ2/ My latest addition. If the Amazon page still lists this at £91.89: I paid way less for this. This is just fantastic. Beautiful, high quality, lovely to hold, brilliantly bright, strobe mode, and with a suitable bezel for clocking someone if you had to. I'd far prefer having this in my hand than a knife.

Finally, I also have a paracord bracelet with fire-starter but I tend not to wear because I feel like they look a bit try-hard sometimes.

Why lock picks? For a start, you'll realise how futile most security is to a determined attacker. But they're also very useful. I've picked into my "security" cabinet when I forgot to bring my keys to work. Opened doors with lost keys. Gas tanks for my brother's bike. Rescued broken keys. Much of this saves time and money. It's fun and most people can learn to use the basics in a day or less. It took me an afternoon with an hour or so pre-reading. Getting great takes years. Getting competent enough to open most of the locks you're likely to encounter takes no time at all.

Group 1:

L-Rake. C-Rake. Short Hook Pick. These are your bread and butter. For most people, a day of reading and practice is enough to become proficient enough with these three tools that you'll be able to open 95% of the locks a normal person is likely to encounter in under 15 minutes maximum. Most often much quicker.

If you want to develop the skill; the short hook is you primary tool. But as a peice of emergency kit for a novice; the rakes will likely be your first port of call for simplicities sake, falling back onto single pin picking if needed.

Group 2:

W-Rake. Diamond Pick. Sometimes the L or C-Rake just aren't working and for some reason a particular lock just seems to work faster with this rake. I primarily use the diamond when working in VERY narrow keyways where even the short hook won't fit. Some people prefer these. Personally, I find them too awkward.

Group 3:

Ball Pick. Half Ball Pick. The Wafer unlockers. Wafer locks (the kind used on basically every locker and filing cabinet) are almost always the simplest locks to pick requiring, in many cases, no skill whatsoever. The pins are like little sliding panels. You put the tension wrench in, push them all down till you feel them "click" (often in no particular order, unlike normal locks), and that's it. Sometimes these locks do require pressure on the panel at the back of the keyway. Hence, the half ball can become preferable if the keyway is small. But in most cases, either of these two will open a wafer lock with some uncoordinated wiggling.

Group 4:

Long Hook Pick. Key Extractor. I don't believe that I have EVER used the long hook as it's almost always too large for the keyway but you never know when you'll encounter that one situation. I've used the key extractor once. It works exactly like it sounds. If someone breaks their key off in the door: you can reach in and pull it out.

Tension Wrenches:

Used to apply turning pressure on the lock, allowing you to feel which pins to press. Possibly the component that requires the most skill in many situations. For example, old rusty locks can be almost completely unresponsive to these, necessitating more complex attacks. The left two have been modified with short ends to allow tension to be provided without filling the keyway making picking smaller locks easier. The bottom right is also twisted to allow different pressure to be applied.

The double-ended pick; I've never quite understood why it was included. It's just a duplicate of two other tools...
